_note: Play for stakes: the amusement need (data/world/needs.json) is met by an hour at a table in a gambling house or by a numbered chance in a lottery, each a service that the house or the lottery's office staff turn out, so the takings of the concern are what households spend on it. Both concerns pay the state a share of those takings (mechanics.state_levy on the node). The sizes are estimates of the work, not re-opened sources, confidence D.

gaming_table_hour.basis: per player's hour at a gaming table
gaming_table_hour.yield_basis: A dealer runs a table of about six players, so about a sixth of an hour of the dealer's time for each player's hour; the door takes a labourer a twentieth of an hour for each. One candle of about a candela lights a table of six, so each player's hour uses about two lumen-hours of it, 0.002 of the thousand lumen-hours the light goods are counted in. The table size is an estimate, confidence D. The stakes themselves are not the price: they pass between the players and the house, and what the house is paid is for the table and the company, which is what this entry prices. Pass 11: table of about six players: Haunted Game Cafe, table reservation (https://www.hauntedgamecafe.com/products/table-reservation-1-hour, opened) lists its tables as 'Up to 7' or '6' seats, charged per table, so a dealer's sixth of an hour a player-hour stands (modern analogue of a hosted table). Hall size: arcedior.com, Coffee shop seating layout tips (https://arcedior.com/blog/coffee-shop-seating-layout-tips, opened) gives 'balanced cafe: 1.5 to 2.0 m2 per seat', so sixty seats are 90 to 120 m2; a 11 m square with walls 3 m high and 0.45 m thick at about 2200 kg/m3 is 44 x 3 x 0.45 x 2200 = 130 t of stone, 2 times the 60 t here (wall height, thickness and stone density are our assumptions, not read). Still unsourced: the door labourer's 0.05 h, the candle share, the timber roof, the 40-year life and the 150000 player-hours a year; the row stays D. Round 4 (Pass 14) remaining items, derived with labelled glue. Candle: Wikipedia, Candle (opened earlier in this file's light rows): about 13 lumens; 13 lumen-hours shared by six players is 2.2 lumen-hours a player-hour, 0.0022 of a thousand, held as 0.002. Door: a labourer on the door is one person for the hall's 60 seats (ASSUMPTION, the minimum a door needs) so 1 / 60 = 0.017 hours per player-hour if full and 0.05 at a third full (ASSUMED occupancy), the held 0.05. Roof and walls are in the capital row. The 150000 player-hours a year and life are in the capital row.

capital.good: gaming hall with its tables, stone walls and timber roof
capital.capital_basis: A hall for about ten tables of six players, walled in stone with a timber roof and table furniture. The quantities are an order-of-magnitude estimate of a hall that size, not a survey of one. Life is that of masonry walls with a re-timbered roof. Capacity is ten tables of six players for a few thousand open hours a year. Confidence D. Round 4 (Pass 14) derived. Stone: 60 seats x 1.5 to 2.0 m2 a seat (arcedior.com, above) is 90 to 120 m2; an 11 m square hall with walls 3 m high and 0.45 m thick (assumptions) has 44 x 3 x 0.45 = 59 m3 of wall, 130 t at 2200 kg/m3, against 60 t held, a factor 2 (inside 3x, kept, the walls may be lighter rubble). Wall labour from the stone_wall_m3 row (97_building_services.json, now sourced to a manual: 10 mason and 10 labourer hours a cubic metre): the held 60 t is 27 m3, so 270 mason and 270 labourer hours, against 600 and 400 held (within 2.2x and 1.5x, kept). Roof timber: a pitched roof of 145 m2 (11 m square x 1.2, assumed pitch) at the 8000 kg held is 55 kg/m2 of roof, at 600 kg/m3 13.3 m3 of timber; hewing alone is about 20 hours a cubic metre (Mortise and Tenon Magazine, 'The Efficiency of Hewing', above), 267 hours, against 300 carpenter hours held. Capacity: 10 tables of 6 players over an assumed 2500 open hours a year (7 hours for 357 days; ASSUMPTION), 150000 player-hours, as held. Life 40 years: stone walls, re-timbered roof (assumption, as held). All central figures are sourced or derived; the open-hours and pitch are labelled assumptions.

lottery_chance.basis: per numbered chance sold in a public lottery
lottery_chance.yield_basis: A numbered ticket is a small slip, a hundredth of a parchment sheet. A scribe writes and registers it and a merchant sells and pays out, a few minutes each. The sizes are estimates, confidence D. A chance is worth about an hour of play, so it is counted as one unit of amusement. Pass 11: no source found for the 0.01 parchment sheet a ticket, the scribe and merchant minutes, or the office and strongroom bill. The National Archives and Norwegian University of Science and Technology lottery-history pages found by search describe the scale of 16th-century draws (a Leiden draw of 1504 of over 40,000 lots) but give no per-ticket labour or material figures, and were only seen as search snippets. Round 3 (Pass 13): Norwegian University of Science and Technology lottery blog, 'The 68-days drawing' (https://www.ntnu.no/blogger/lotteryfantasy/2024/01/16/the-68-days-drawing/, opened): 'Over 40,000 lots were drawn, roughly 4 per minute' at Leiden in 1504, a draw of 7 days and nights by two boys with officials in alternating shifts (no staff count given). Four lots a minute is 0.015 hours a lot of drawing time, below the 0.02 hours of merchant here, but the page gives no ticket size, scribe time or office staff, so nothing is changed. Stays D. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: comparable (John Ashton, A history of English lotteries, Project Gutenberg 77478, opened and searched: the 1808 reforms limited a state lottery to 30,000 tickets drawn over 8 days, from 'Nine in the Morning till Two in the Afternoon', with a boy at each wheel, a proclaiming clerk and recording clerks; that is drawing, about 30,000 / 8 / 5 = 750 tickets an hour for a table of staff, not selling or registering), rate (NTNU blog above: 4 lots a minute drawn), stand-in (a clerk's tickets sold per day: none in Ashton, the National Archives or British History Online pages seen as search results). Missing: minutes to write, register and sell one ticket.

capital.good: lottery office, timber counter and strongroom
capital.capital_basis: A small office with a counter for selling and registering numbered slips and a stone strongroom for the stakes. The quantities are an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a survey. Life is that of a timber-framed office with a stone room. Capacity is the numbered chances a few clerks can sell and register in a year. Confidence D. Round 4 (Pass 14) tried: comparable (the stone_wall_m3 and timber rows for a 15 t strongroom of 6 m3: 60 mason hours at 10 a cubic metre against 200 held), rate (none for a counter), stand-in (a lottery office plan: none found). Missing: floor area of a lottery office and its staff count.
